facts.title: Heaviest Element Ever Made
facts.text: Oganesson is element 118, the heaviest element confirmed to exist and the one with the highest atomic number on the periodic table. With 118 protons crammed into its nucleus, it completes the seventh period of the table. No element beyond it has yet been officially recognized.

facts.title: Named for a Living Scientist
facts.text: Oganesson honors the Russian-Armenian physicist Yuri Oganessian, a pioneer of superheavy-element research at the Joint Institute for Nuclear Research in Dubna. When it was named in 2016, he became only the second person ever to have an element named after them while still alive, after Glenn Seaborg (seaborgium). The symbol Og and the '-on' ending mirror the noble gases like neon and argon.

facts.title: Made by Fusing Calcium and Californium
facts.text: Scientists created oganesson by firing a beam of calcium-48 ions at a target of californium-249 at the Dubna cyclotron in Russia, in collaboration with the U.S. Lawrence Livermore and Oak Ridge labs. Out of trillions upon trillions of collisions, only a handful of atoms were ever produced. The discovery was first reported in 2002 and 2005, and confirmed in the years that followed.

facts.title: Only a Few Atoms Exist
facts.text: In total, scientists have detected only about five or six atoms of oganesson in history. Each one was identified not directly but by tracing the chain of alpha-particle decays it left behind. This makes it one of the rarest substances humans have ever observed.

facts.title: Vanishes in Under a Millisecond
facts.text: Oganesson is extraordinarily unstable: its most studied isotope, oganesson-294, has a half-life of roughly 0.7 milliseconds before it decays by emitting an alpha particle. That is far less than the blink of an eye, which lasts about a tenth of a second. Such fleeting lifetimes are why superheavy atoms must be detected almost the instant they form.

facts.title: A Noble Gas That May Not Be Noble
facts.text: Oganesson sits beneath radon in the noble-gas column, so by tradition it should be chemically inert. But theory suggests relativistic effects on its electrons could make it surprisingly reactive, unlike helium or neon. Some calculations even predict it would be a solid, not a gas, at room temperature.

facts.title: Where Relativity Rewrites Chemistry
facts.text: In such a heavy atom, the innermost electrons move at a large fraction of the speed of light, so Einstein's relativity must be used to describe them. These relativistic effects are predicted to smear out oganesson's electron shells, possibly blurring the neat shell structure seen in lighter elements. Physicists study it precisely because it tests the limits of our quantum and relativistic theories of the atom.

facts.title: Not Found Anywhere in Nature
facts.text: Oganesson does not occur naturally on Earth, in meteorites, or anywhere known in the cosmos, because it decays far too quickly to persist. Every atom that has ever existed was deliberately manufactured by physicists in a particle accelerator. It is a purely human-made addition to the universe's catalogue of matter.

facts.title: No Uses Beyond Pure Science
facts.text: Because it exists only as a few short-lived atoms, oganesson has no industrial, medical, or commercial applications whatsoever. Its entire value is scientific: helping researchers probe how the periodic table behaves at its extreme edge. Studying it guides the search for even heavier, possibly more stable elements.

facts.title: Hunting the Island of Stability
facts.text: Oganesson lies near a long-theorized 'island of stability,' a region where certain superheavy nuclei with special numbers of protons and neutrons might survive far longer than their neighbors. While oganesson itself is fleeting, its creation is a stepping stone toward isotopes that could last seconds, minutes, or more. This quest drives laboratories in Russia, Germany, the United States, and Japan to keep pushing the periodic table's frontier.
